text:
So instead of predicting the bubble, here's what I'd check in my own portfolio this week. Not advice, just a checklist.

One. Open your ETF's factsheet and look at the top ten and the country weights. Know what you actually own.

Two. Set your mix of stocks and bonds by when you need the money, not by the headlines.

Three. If you diversify away from the giants, with equal weight or more Europe, do it for the long run, knowing it can lag for a decade.

Four. Automate your monthly plan, so a scary headline can't stop it. In this replay, pausing for five years cost more than any crash.

And five. Write down today what you'll do if your portfolio drops forty percent. Decide now, while you're calm, because you won't be then.

So, is AI a bubble? Honestly, I don't know, and neither does anyone on YouTube who tells you they do.

And here's the part the doom videos leave out. Valuation is a terrible timing tool.

In January 2018, the Shiller CAPE was already around thirty-three. Plenty of people said the market was too expensive, and sold.

If you had sold your world ETF at the end of 2017 for that reason, you would have missed a gain of one hundred and seventy-five percent since then.

Expensive markets can get more expensive for years. That's why the answer to a possible bubble isn't selling. It's building a portfolio you can hold either way.

Even if it is, that doesn't make AI fake. The internet wasn't fake either. But between 1999 and 2001, Amazon's share price still fell more than ninety percent.

Being right about the technology is not the same as being right about the price.

What twenty-seven years of euro data does show is this.

One. A bubble can cost a lump sum investor thirteen years, even in the whole world index.

Two. In a full crash, swapping one stock index for another barely helps. Owning bonds or cash, matched to when you need the money, does.

Three. Behaviour mattered more than any fund choice. Keeping a monthly plan running, and not selling, beat every clever alternative in this video.

If your portfolio dropped forty-five percent next year, would you sell, stop buying, or keep going? Tell me honestly in the comments.

If you only remember one thing from this video: the market decided how deep the hole was. Investors decided whether they climbed out.

Sources and method are in the description. This isn't financial advice, and past returns don't guarantee future ones.
